primary_meaning: bondage/slavery to sin and the world system opposed to God, from which God delivers His people
primary_basis: Exodus 1–14 (Israel's enslavement under Pharaoh and the exodus deliverance)
Deuteronomy 5:6; 6:12; 8:14; 13:5, 10 (repeated formula of YHWH who brought Israel out of Egypt, the house of bondage)
Hosea 11:1 cited in Matthew 2:15 (typological 'out of Egypt I called my son')
1 Corinthians 10:1–11 (Paul's use of the exodus generation as types for Christian life and warning against returning to sin)
Revelation 11:8 (spiritual 'Egypt' as the place where the Lord was crucified, linking to worldly opposition)

alternatives.meaning: temporary place of refuge, protection, or material provision
basis: Genesis 12:10; 37–50 (Abraham and especially Joseph's family preserved in Egypt during famine)
Matthew 2:13–15 (holy family's flight to Egypt to escape Herod)
occasional prophetic or historical notes of Egypt as asylum

alternatives.meaning: idolatry, pagan power, and object of divine judgment
basis: Exodus 12:12; Numbers 33:4 (judgment on the gods of Egypt)
Isaiah 19; Jeremiah 46; Ezekiel 29–32 (oracles against Egypt as proud empire and false security)
Isaiah 31:1–3 (warning against trusting Egypt's horses and chariots rather than YHWH)

alternatives.meaning: the flesh or carnal nature (in some allegorical or puritan traditions)
basis: extended typology of Pharaoh as the flesh/sin nature and Egypt as its domain (building on Exodus and 1 Cor 10)
occasional homiletic or devotional readings equating return to Egypt with fleshly living

notes: Across patristic, medieval, Reformation, and modern evangelical/biblical-studies sources the dominant symbolic register is negative (bondage/world/opposition), grounded in the exodus paradigm; positive or neutral uses (refuge, provision) are secondary and usually limited to specific narratives. No major Christian tradition treats Egypt as a settled positive symbol of the people of God.
